# Finding the Gain K at Imaginary Axis Intersection

## Setting Up the Problem

The characteristic equation from the denominator of $T(s)$ is:

$$(1-K)s^2 + 2(1-K)s + (2-K) = 0$$

The Routh table (first column) gives:

$$\text{Row } s^2: \;(1-K), \quad \text{Row } s^1: \;2(1-K), \quad \text{Row } s^0: \;(2-K)$$

## Applying the Routh Stability Criterion

The system is **stable** when all first-column elements share the same sign. A **sign change** or **zero** in the first column marks the boundary where poles cross the imaginary axis.

Setting each first-column element to zero:

| Element | Zero when |
|---|---|
| $1 - K$ | $K = 1$ |
| $2(1-K)$ | $K = 1$ |
| $2 - K$ | $K = 2$ |

### Checking $K = 1$ (entire-row-of-zeros case)

At $K=1$, both the $s^2$ and $s^1$ rows vanish simultaneously. The characteristic equation collapses to $1 = 0$ (degenerate), meaning the poles go to **infinity** — not a finite imaginary-axis crossing.

### Checking $K = 2$ (single zero in the $s^0$ row)

At $K=2$ the Routh table becomes:

$$\begin{bmatrix} s^2 & -1 & 0 \\ s^1 & -2 & 0 \\ s^0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

The first element of the $s^0$ row is **zero**, signalling marginal stability. The **auxiliary equation** is formed from the row directly above ($s^1$):

$$2(1-2)\,s + 0 = -2s = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; s = 0$$

This places a closed-loop pole exactly **on the imaginary axis** (at the origin).

## Verification by Direct Substitution

At $K=2$ the characteristic equation is:

$$-s^2 - 2s + 0 = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; s(s+2)=0$$

$$s_1 = 0, \qquad s_2 = -2$$

Indeed $s_1 = 0$ lies on the imaginary axis, confirming the Routh-table result.

## Conclusion

The root locus intersects the imaginary axis when:

$$\boxed{2}$$
